en: Tattvabodha 1; Sādhanacatuṣṭaya 2; Tattvaviveka.
3. The three bodies; 4. The organs of perception;
5. The organs of action.
6. The three states; 7. The five sheaths; 8. The Self.
9. The manner of the arising of the twenty-four principles;
10. The cognition of the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara); 11. The identity of the individual soul and the Lord.
12. Liberation while living (jīvanmukti).
13. Having bowed to the Lord of Yogīs, Vāsudeva, the Guru who bestows knowledge, [one should perform] the rites.
For the benefit of those seeking liberation, the awakening to reality is here set forth.

We shall now describe the method for the discrimination of reality (*tattva-viveka*), which serves as the means to liberation for those qualified aspirants who possess the fourfold prerequisites (*sādhana-catuṣṭaya*). The fourfold prerequisites: [to be detailed below].
What is the fourfold means? 1.1 Discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities;
1.2 Dispassion toward the enjoyment of the fruits of objects here and hereafter.
1.3 The perfection of the six qualities beginning with tranquility (śama).
1.4 And the desire for liberation (mumukṣutva). 1.1.1 Viveka (discrimination).
What is the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities?
The one eternal entity is Brahman; everything other than that is non-eternal.
This alone is the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities.
1.1.2 What is detachment (*vairāgya*)? It is the absence of desire for the enjoyments of this world and heaven.
1.1.3 What is the perfection of the means such as tranquility?
It is tranquility (śama), self-restraint (dama), withdrawal (uparati), endurance (titikṣā), faith (śraddhā), and concentration (samādhāna). 1.1.3.1 Tranquility (śama).
What is tranquility (*śama*)? It is the restraint of the mind. What is self-control (*dama*)? [It is the restraint of the external senses. 1.1.3.2–3.2.
What is cessation?
It is precisely the performance of one's own duty.
1.1.3–4. Forbearance.
What is *titikṣā*? It is the endurance of cold, heat, pleasure, pain, and so forth. [Sūtra 1.1.3] What is *śraddhā*? [Sūtra 1.1.5]
What is faith (*śraddhā*)? Faith is conviction in the words of the Guru, the Vedānta, and so forth.
1.1.3.6 Samādhāna (Resolution).
What is concentration? It is one-pointedness of mind.
1.4 [The desire for liberation].
What is the desire for liberation (*mumukṣutva*)?
It is the wish: "May liberation be mine.
These constitute the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*).
Consequently, they become qualified for the discernment of reality (tattva-viveka). What is this discernment of reality?
"The Self is truth; everything other than that is false.
|| 2.2 || Who is the Self?
It is distinct from the gross, subtle, and causal bodies, and transcends the five sheaths (pañcakośa).
That which exists as the witness of the three states, whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda), and which remains as the Pure Being— that is the Self.
3.0 The Three Bodies.
3.1 What is the gross body?

It is the body composed of the five great elements in their quintuplicated form (pañcīkṛta), produced by past actions (satkarma), and serving as the locus for the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth.
This gross body undergoes six modifications: it exists, is born, grows, transforms, decays, and perishes.
What, then, is the subtle body?
That which is composed of the five great elements in their unquintuplicated state, produced by past actions (*satkarma*),
and serving as the means for the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth, consists of the five organs of knowledge,
the five organs of action, the five vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and others, and the single mind (*manas*).
And the intellect (*buddhi*), being one, together with the seventeen constituents (*kalā*), that which thus exists is the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*).
What is the causal body (*kāraṇa-śarīra*)?
That which exists as non-discernible, beginningless ignorance (avidyā) in nature, being merely the cause of the two bodies,
and consisting of the non-discriminative form of the lack of knowledge regarding one's true nature—
that is the causal body (kāraṇa-śarīra).
4||0 The organs of cognition (jñānendriya).
4||1 The ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose—these are the five organs of cognition.
4||1||0 The presiding deities of the organs of cognition.
4.1.1 The deity of the ear is the quarters (diś). 4.1.2 Of the skin is Vāyu. 4.1.3 Of the eye is Sūrya.
4|1|4 Varuṇa is the deity of the tongue;
4|1|5 the two Aśvins are the deities of the nose.
Thus [are] the deities of the organs of knowledge.
4.2 Objects of the Cognitive Faculties 4.2.1 The object of the auditory faculty is the apprehension of sound.
4.2.2 The object of the tactile faculty is the apprehension of touch.
4|2|3 The object of the eye is the apprehension of form. 4|2|4 The object of the tongue is the apprehension of taste.
4|2|5 The object of the nose is the apprehension of odor.
5||0 The organs of action:
5||1 Speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals—these are the five organs of action.
5||1||0 The deities of the organs of action.
5|1|1 Vahni is the deity of speech;
5|1|2 Indra is the deity of the two hands;
5|1|3 Viṣṇu is the deity of the two feet.
5|1|4: Death is the deity of the anus; 5|1|5: Prajāpati is the deity of the generative organ. Thus end the deities of the organs of action.
5.2 Objects of the organs of action (karmendriya).
5.2.1 The object of speech is speaking. 5.2.2 The object of the two hands is grasping objects.
5|2|3: The object of the feet is locomotion; 5|2|4: The object of the anus is the evacuation of waste; 5|2|5: The object of the generative organ is pleasure.
6||0 What are the three states? 6||1 They are the waking, dreaming, and deep sleep states.
6.1.1 What is the waking state? That which is known through the organs of perception, such as the ears, and through objects of perception, such as sound, is the waking state.
6|1|1 The Self that identifies with the gross body is called Viśva.
6|1|2 If it is asked, "What is the state of dreaming? [it is that which] was seen or heard during the waking state.

The state of dream is that manifold world (*prapañca*) which is perceived during sleep due to the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) produced by that [waking state]. The self (*ātman*) who identifies with the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*) is called *taijasa*.
6|1|3 Therefore, what is the state of deep sleep?
The state of deep sleep is that wherein one thinks, "I know nothing at all; I am experiencing sleep with happiness."
The Self that identifies with the causal body (kāraṇa-śarīra) is called the Prājña.
What are the five sheaths (pañca-kośas)? Which are the five sheaths?
It consists of food (*annamaya*), vital breath (*prāṇamaya*), mind (*manomaya*), consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), and bliss (*ānandamaya*).
What is that which consists of food?
Having become through the essence of food alone, and having attained growth through the essence of food alone...
That which dissolves into the earth, which consists of food, is the sheath consisting of food,
the gross body. What is the sheath consisting of vital breath?
The five vital airs, beginning with prāṇa, and the pentad of organs beginning with speech constitute the sheath consisting of prāṇa (prāṇamaya-kośa).
What is the sheath consisting of mind (manomaya-kośa)?
That which arises from the mind together with the five organs of cognition is the sheath consisting of mind (manomaya-kośa).
What is the sheath consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya)?
That which arises from the combination of the five organs of intellect and knowledge is the sheath consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya-kośa). What is the sheath consisting of bliss (ānandamaya)?

In the same way, the sheath consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya-kośa*) is the impure *sattva* residing within ignorance (*avidyā*), which constitutes the causal body (*kāraṇa-śarīra*), accompanied by the functions of "dear" and so forth.
This is the pentad of sheaths.
8. "O Self, my body, my vital breaths, my mind,
my intellect, and my ignorance are known by the self alone."
For example,
just as bracelets, earrings, houses, and so forth, which are known as "mine," are distinct from oneself, so too the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*) and so forth are distinct from oneself.
The self, when known as "mine," does not truly exist.
8|1 What, then, is the Self? It is that whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
8|1|1 What is existence?
That which exists even in the three periods of time is *sat*. What is consciousness (*cit*)? It is that whose nature is knowledge (*jñāna*).
8|1|3 What is bliss? It is the nature of happiness. 8|2 Thus, one should know one's own Self as having the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda).
9||0 Now we shall explain the manner of the arising of the twenty-four principles (tattvas).
9||1 There exists Māyā, which has Brahman as its substratum and consists of the qualities (guṇas) of sattva, rajas, and tamas.
9||1||1 From that, space (ākāśa) was produced.
9.1.2 From space, air; 9.1.3 from air, fire; 9.1.4 from fire, water.
9.1.5 From water comes earth.
9.2 Regarding the origin of the organs of knowledge,
among these five elements:
9.2.1 From the *sāttvika* portion of space, the sense organ of hearing (*śrotra*) was produced.
9.2.2 From the *sāttvika* portion of air, the sense organ of touch (*tvak*) was produced. 9.2.3 From the *sāttvika* portion of fire, the sense organ of sight (*cakṣus*) was produced.
9||2||4 The sense of taste is produced from the *sāttvika* portion of water.
9||2||5 The sense of smell is produced from the *sāttvika* portion of earth.
9||3 From the collective *sāttvika* portion of these five elements...
The internal organs—mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*)—have arisen.
9||3||1 Mind consists of volition and doubt. 9||3||2 Intellect consists of determination.
9||3||3 The ego-maker is the *ahaṃkāra*. 9||3||4 The thinker is the *citta*. 9||4 The deities of the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
9.4.1 The deity of the mind is the Moon; 9.4.2 of the intellect, Brahmā;
9.4.3 of the ego, Rudra.
9|4 Vāsudeva is of the mind.
9|5 Regarding the manifestation of the organs of action,
among these five principles:

9.5.1 From the rājasa portion of space, the organ of speech was produced. 9.5.2 From the rājasa portion of air, the organ of the hands was produced. 9.5.3 From the rājasa portion of fire, the organ of the feet was produced.
9.5.4 From the *rajas* portion of water, the organ of generation (*upasthendriya*) was produced. 9.5.5 From the *rajas* portion of earth, the organ of excretion (*gudendriya*) was produced.
9.5.6 From the collective *rajas* portion of these [elements], the five vital breaths (*pañcaprāṇāḥ*) were produced.
9||6 The Origination of the Five Elements 9||6||1 From the tamasic portion of these five elements, the five elements in their quintuplicated (pañcīkṛta) state arise.
If it is asked, "How is the quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*) performed?
[the answer is: Having divided each one of these five great elements—which consist of portions of *tamas*—into two parts, one half of each is set aside separately.
Having established [the first half] in silence, one should divide each subsequent half into four parts and perform the conjunction of one's own quarter-part with the other three halves; in that way,
the quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa) occurs.

9.6.3 From these five gross elements, having been quintuplicated (pañcīkṛta), the physical body (sthūla-śarīra) arises. 9.6.4 Thus, the identity between the individual body (piṇḍa) and the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is established.
10.0 The cognition of difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara).
10.1 That which is the reflection of Brahman known as the individual soul (jīva), characterized by identification with the gross body,
perceives the Lord as distinct from itself due to its own nature.
10.2 When the Self has ignorance as its limiting adjunct (upādhi), it is called the individual soul (jīva). 10.3 When it has māyā as its limiting adjunct, it is called the Lord (īśvara).
10.4 Thus, as long as the perception of a distinction between the individual soul and the Lord persists due to the difference in their limiting adjuncts, [so long does that state endure].
Until that point, saṃsāra—in the form of birth, death, and so forth—does not cease.
Therefore, for this reason, one should not accept the notion of difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (Īśvara). [This is] the oneness of the individual soul and the Lord.

Now, how can there arise in both— the individual soul (*jīva*), who possesses ego and is partially ignorant, and the Lord (*īśvara*), who is devoid of ego and omniscient— a cognition of non-difference from the Great Sentence, "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*)?
If it is argued that [the two are different] because they are pervaded by contradictory attributes, we say no.

The referent of the term *tvam* (thou) is the consciousness that identifies with the gross and subtle bodies; whereas pure consciousness is that which is free from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and attained during the state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
The referent indicated by the word *tvaṃ* (thou) is [the inner self].

11.2 Thus, the Lord (*īśvara*), characterized by omniscience and other attributes, is the denoted meaning (*vācyārtha*) of the word *tat* (that). Pure consciousness (*śuddhacaitanya*), devoid of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is the referent indicated by the word *tat*.
11.3 Thus, there is no sublation of the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) in their nature as consciousness.
12.0 Liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*).

And thus, the meaning is that those in whom the realization of Brahman has arisen toward all beings through the Vedānta texts and the instruction of a true guru are *jīvanmuktas* (liberated while living).
12.1 Now, who is a *jīvanmukta*?
Just as there is the firm conviction, "I am the body," "I am a man," "I am a Brāhmaṇa," or "I am a Śūdra," so too [there is the realization]: "I am not a Brāhmaṇa, nor a Śūdra, nor a man;
rather, I am unattached, whose nature is existence-consciousness-bliss (saccidānanda), and whose form is light."

One who possesses immediate realization (aparokṣajñāna) through the firm conviction, "I am the inner witness of all, whose nature is the space of consciousness," is a liberated-while-living (jīvanmukta).
12||2 By means of the direct knowledge that "I am indeed Brahman," one becomes completely liberated from the bondage of all actions.
13||0 If it is asked, "What are actions? And how many kinds of actions are there?"
13||1 Karma exists in three types, distinguished as future (*āgāmin*), accumulated (*sañcita*), and commenced (*prārabdha*).
13||1||1 That merit and demerit in the form of action performed by the body of the knower (*jñānin*) immediately after the arising of knowledge is designated as "future."

13||1||2 What is accumulated karma (*sañcita-karma*)? That collection of actions previously acquired which remains, serving as the seed for infinite millions of births— that is to be known as the accumulated.
13.1.3 If it is asked what *prārabdha-karma* is:
that karma which, having produced this body, bestows such things as pleasure and pain in this very world, is *prārabdha*.
That which has been set in motion (*prārabdha-karma*) is destroyed through experience; for the exhaustion of *prārabdha-karma* occurs only through experience.

(13.2) Accumulated karma (*sañcita-karma*) is destroyed by the knowledge consisting of the firm conviction "I am indeed Brahman. (13.3) Future karma (*āgāmi-karma*) is also destroyed by knowledge; furthermore, regarding future karmas—
Like water on a lotus leaf, there is no attachment for the wise.
Furthermore, whatever future merit arises from those who praise, worship, or serve the wise, that merit accrues to them.
13:5 All the future and present unspeakable sinful actions performed by those who revile, hate, or inflict suffering upon the man of knowledge pass away from him.
13.6 Likewise, the knower of the Self, having crossed over saṃsāra, attains the bliss of Brahman even here in this world;
for the Śruti says, "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow.
13.7 Whether he casts off his body in Kāśī or in the house of an outcaste, [he attains liberation].
"And from the Smṛti: 'At the moment of attaining knowledge, he is liberated, his latent desires having vanished.
Thus ends the chapter on the awakening to reality.
